centuries.text: Writing and the first cities spread in Mesopotamia; Egypt is unified under its first dynasties around 3100 BC. Farming villages cover much of Eurasia, Africa and the Americas, but most people live outside any state.
City-states such as Uruk, Ur and Kish compete in Sumer. Egypt's Early Dynastic kings rule the Nile valley from Memphis.
Sumerian city-states grow and trade widely. In the Indus valley, settlements are growing toward the cities of the Harappan civilisation.
Egypt's Old Kingdom begins and builds the first stone pyramids. Sumerian kings record their deeds in cuneiform.
The great pyramids of Giza are built in Egypt. Harappan cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa flourish in the Indus valley.
Egypt's Old Kingdom and the Indus cities are at their height. Early Bronze Age cultures spread across Europe and China's Longshan culture builds walled towns.
Sumerian city-states fight over land and water. Ebla in Syria is a major trading power.
Sargon of Akkad unites Mesopotamia in what is often called the first empire. Egypt's Old Kingdom is in its last long reigns.
The Akkadian Empire collapses and Egypt's Old Kingdom breaks up, at a time of drought across the region. The Indus cities begin a slow decline.
The Third Dynasty of Ur revives Sumerian rule in Mesopotamia. Egypt is divided between rival centres.
Egypt is reunited under the Middle Kingdom. Minoan palaces rise on Crete, and Bronze Age China sees the traditional start of the Xia dynasty.
Amorite kingdoms rule much of Mesopotamia. Assyrian merchants run a trade network into Anatolia.
Hammurabi of Babylon unites much of Mesopotamia and issues his law code. The Indus cities are largely abandoned.
The Hyksos take control of northern Egypt. The Hittites rise in Anatolia.
The Shang dynasty rules the Yellow River valley in China. Mycenaean Greece and the Hittite kingdom grow; Egypt drives out the Hyksos.
Egypt's New Kingdom builds an empire into the Levant and Nubia. The Mitanni, Hittites and Kassite Babylon are the other great powers of the Near East.
Egypt, the Hittites, Mitanni, Babylon and Assyria trade letters and gifts as great powers. Mycenaean palaces dominate Greece.
Egypt and the Hittites fight for Syria and make one of the earliest known peace treaties. Shang China leaves the first written records on oracle bones.
The Late Bronze Age collapse destroys the Hittite kingdom, Mycenaean palaces and many cities of the eastern Mediterranean. The Olmec culture develops in Mexico.
Small kingdoms and city-states replace the fallen empires of the Near East. In China the Zhou overthrow the Shang around 1046 BC.
Iron working spreads. Phoenician cities trade across the Mediterranean; Israel and Judah form kingdoms; Zhou kings rule much of northern China.
The Neo-Assyrian Empire begins to expand. Phoenicians found trading posts in the western Mediterranean.
Greek city-states grow and found colonies; Carthage is founded by Phoenicians. Zhou royal power weakens in China.
Assyria rules most of the Near East. Rome is a small city in Italy; Kush rules Egypt for a time.
Babylon replaces Assyria; the Persian Achaemenid Empire is founded by Cyrus the Great around 550 BC. The Buddha and Confucius teach in this period.
Persia rules from Egypt to the Indus and fights the Greek city-states. China is divided among warring states; Rome becomes a republic.
Greek city-states exhaust each other in war. Alexander the Great conquers Persia in the 330s BC and his empire splits after his death.
Hellenistic kingdoms rule the eastern Mediterranean; the Maurya Empire unites most of India. Qin unifies China in 221 BC and the Han follow.
Rome defeats Carthage and expands around the Mediterranean. Han China fights the Xiongnu and opens routes into Central Asia.
Rome's republic falls into civil wars and becomes an empire under Augustus. Han China and Parthia are the other great powers of Eurasia.
The Roman and Han empires dominate the two ends of Eurasia. Christianity begins in Roman Judaea.
The Roman Empire reaches its greatest extent under Trajan. The Kushan Empire rules Central Asia and northern India.
Han China collapses into the Three Kingdoms. Rome suffers civil wars and invasions; the Sasanian dynasty replaces the Parthians in Persia.
Constantine favours Christianity and founds Constantinople. The Gupta Empire rises in India; northern China is ruled by many short-lived states.
The Western Roman Empire falls to Germanic kingdoms; the Eastern Empire survives. Huns raid Europe and India.
Justinian reconquers parts of the West for the Eastern Roman Empire. China is reunited under the Sui in 589.
Islam begins in Arabia and the early caliphates conquer the Middle East, North Africa and Persia. Tang China is the largest state in East Asia.
The Umayyad and then Abbasid caliphates rule from Spain to Central Asia. The Franks rise in western Europe; the Tang are at their height.
Charlemagne is crowned emperor in 800. The Abbasids rule from Baghdad; Vikings raid Europe.
The Tang dynasty ends in 907; the caliphate splits into rival states. The Holy Roman Empire is founded in 962.
Song China is the richest state in the world. The Seljuk Turks take much of the Middle East; Europe launches the First Crusade in 1096.
Crusader states hold parts of the Levant. The Jin conquer northern China; the Khmer Empire builds Angkor Wat.
The Mongols under Genghis Khan and his successors conquer the largest land empire in history. The Delhi Sultanate rules northern India.
The Black Death kills a large share of the population of Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. The Ming replace the Mongol Yuan in China in 1368.
The Ottomans take Constantinople in 1453. The Aztec and Inca empires expand; Portuguese ships explore Africa and Columbus reaches the Americas in 1492.
Spain conquers the Aztec and Inca empires. The Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal empires dominate the Islamic world; the Reformation divides western Christianity.
European trading companies set up in Asia and colonies in the Americas. The Qing replace the Ming in China; Tokugawa Japan limits foreign contact.
Britain and France fight for empire worldwide. Revolutions in America and France end the century; the Mughal Empire declines.
Latin America becomes independent, industry transforms Britain and then other countries, and European powers colonise most of Africa and much of Asia.
Two world wars, the end of European colonial empires, the Cold War and the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991 reshape the world.
Global trade and the internet connect the world. China grows into a great power; wars continue in the Middle East and Ukraine.
